claims.text: Substituting approximately 5–10 at.% copper for one principal element will improve the heat-transfer capability of the high-entropy alloy.
The proposed copper substitution will preserve the alloy's structural integrity under reactor conditions.
The baseline intermediate-layer alloy contains multiple refractory and corrosion-resistant elements.
Replacing part of a constituent with copper will create a copper-enriched dispersion in the alloy matrix.
Copper substitution will produce a refined copper-rich phase.
The copper-rich phase will be uniformly dispersed within the high-entropy alloy matrix.
The dispersed copper-rich phase will provide enhanced electronic heat-conduction pathways.
The copper-rich dispersion will maintain grain-boundary cohesion.
The copper-rich dispersion will maintain overall phase stability.
Copper has inherently high electronic thermal conductivity.
Copper's electronic thermal conductivity will facilitate more efficient heat transfer through the alloy.
At 5–10 at.% substitution, copper will not adversely affect the alloy microstructure.
At 5–10 at.% substitution, copper will not adversely affect the alloy's load-bearing capability.
The copper-modified alloy will have approximately 20–30% higher effective thermal conductivity than the undoped alloy.
The yield strength of the copper-modified alloy will remain within approximately 10% of the baseline value.
The fracture toughness of the copper-modified alloy will remain within approximately 10% of the baseline value.
The predicted improvements will hold at approximately 600–900°C under representative plasma-facing mechanical loads and irradiation exposure.
The predicted improvements are not asserted to hold outside 600–900°C or outside the specified loading and irradiation conditions.
